claims.text: Photos posted by depressed individuals tend to have higher hue values (bluer) compared to photos posted by healthy individuals.
Photos posted by depressed individuals tend to have lower saturation values (grayer) compared to photos posted by healthy individuals.
Photos posted by depressed individuals tend to have lower brightness values (darker) compared to photos posted by healthy individuals.
Depressed individuals are less likely to apply Instagram filters to their posted photographs than healthy individuals.
When applying Instagram filters, depressed individuals most disproportionately favor the Inkwell black-and-white filter.
Depressed participants are more likely than healthy participants to post photos containing human faces.
Photos posted by depressed participants contain a lower average face count per photograph than photos posted by healthy participants.
The All-data Random Forest classifier achieved a depression recall of 0.697, compared to general practitioners' unassisted diagnostic recall of 0.510.
Predictive markers of depression are detectable in Instagram posts made prior to the date of first clinical diagnosis.
Human ratings of photo sadness and happiness show extremely low correlation with computationally extracted image features.

evidence.description: Increased hue predicted depression with positive regression coefficients in both All-data (coef = .325) and Pre-diagnosis (coef = .802) Bayesian logistic regression models.
Decreased saturation predicted depression with negative regression coefficients in both All-data (coef = -.602) and Pre-diagnosis (coef = -.271) models.
Decreased brightness predicted depression with negative regression coefficients in both All-data (coef = -.572) and Pre-diagnosis (coef = -.209) models.
Filter usage was negatively associated with depression status in both All-data (coef = -.124) and Pre-diagnosis (coef = -.071) regression models.
Chi-squared analysis showed depressed participants disproportionately favored the Inkwell filter compared to expected usage frequencies (p < .001).
The presence of a face ('Has face') positively predicted depression in both All-data (coef = .243) and Pre-diagnosis (coef = .267) models.
'Face count' negatively predicted depression in both All-data (coef = -.105) and Pre-diagnosis (coef = -.207) models.
A 1200-tree Random Forest classifier achieved a recall of .697 (SD .008) vs general practitioner recall of .510 from meta-analysis benchmark.
The Pre-diagnosis Random Forest model using only posts made prior to first diagnosis achieved precision of .541 and specificity of .833.
Pearson product-moment correlation matrix showed correlations near zero between human affective ratings (happy, sad) and computational features (hue, saturation, brightness).

methodologies.name: Computational feature extraction and Random Forest classification
methodologies.description: Extracted pixel-level HSV color statistics, metadata features, and algorithmic face counts from Instagram user posting histories to train Bayesian logistic regression and Random Forest models for depression screening.
conditions: Pre-diagnosis model (posts prior to clinical diagnosis)
Human ratings subset (13,184 photos rated on MTurk)

limitations.text: Prior health-screening studies on social media relied exclusively on text analysis and did not harness visual data.
The study used a broad clinical definition of depression without acquiring specific diagnostic sub-class or comorbidity details.
The participant sample consisted of individuals who sought clinical care and agreed to share social media data, limiting broad inferences to all depressed individuals.
Socio-technical predictive models degrade over time as data trends change, requiring frequent recalibration.
Forty-three percent of survey participants refused to share Instagram data due to data privacy concerns.

future_work.text: Integrate textual analysis of Instagram comments, captions, and tags alongside visual feature modeling.
Adjust questionnaires in future studies to acquire specific diagnostic class and comorbidity information.
Establish stronger participant confidence regarding data security and privacy in social media research.
